lead: Alaska plumbing is built for deep cold, long distances and frozen ground. PipeMend sends licensed local plumbers from Anchorage to Fairbanks and Juneau.
risk: frozen water and sewer lines, heat tape and boiler failures, and well and septic systems in rural areas
why: Alaska's winters push frost deep into the ground, and in the Interior some homes sit on permafrost. Water and sewer lines must be buried deep, insulated or heat-traced, and a power outage or failed heat tape can freeze them within hours.

Many homes heat with oil or gas boilers, which often heat domestic water too. Outside the larger cities, homes rely on wells, holding tanks and septic systems, and a plumber may drive a long way to reach them. Alaska licenses plumbers through state certificates of fitness and mechanical administrator licenses.
problems: Fairbanks, the Mat-Su and the Interior
tips: Check heat tape before winter and keep a backup heat source.
Never let a home's heat drop low during a cold snap.
Know how to drain the system if you lose heat for a long time.
Keep crawl-space vents closed in winter.
areas: Calls come from Anchorage, the Mat-Su Valley, Fairbanks and the Interior, Juneau, the Kenai Peninsula and Southeast Alaska.

faq.q: How do I keep pipes from freezing in an Alaska winter?
faq.a: Keep the heat on, keep crawl spaces closed, and make sure heat tape on vulnerable lines works. If you leave for a long time, have a plumber drain and winterize the system. A temperature alarm that texts you is cheap insurance.

licensing: Plumbers need a state certificate of fitness from the Alaska Department of Labor, and plumbing businesses need a mechanical administrator license.
